narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class that year, far below the average ranking of students who were accepted. Your first-year class ranking also worked against you, though to a lesser degree; you again finished in the bottom decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile.

Your LSAT score was the only major factor that pulled in the opposite direction. At 41, it sits noticeably above the average score of 37 among accepted students and therefore helped reduce the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your two class-rank indicators.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance in law school was likely to be weaker than most admitted students, making success on the bar exam uncertain.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your study habits and academic performance immediately. Raising your grades in the remaining years will directly strengthen any future applications and also better prepare you for the bar exam itself. Consider seeking academic support or tutoring now so that your class rankings improve before you reapply.
